'''Dermontti Farra Dawson''' (born June 17, 1965) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Center (gridiron football)|center]] and [[long snapper]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] with the [[Kentucky Wildcats football|Kentucky Wildcats]]. He was selected by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] in the second round of the [[1988 NFL draft]] and spent his entire pro career with the team and was elected to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2012.

'''Deron Leigh Cherry''' (born September 12, 1959) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Safety (gridiron football position)|safety]] for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1981 to 1991. Cherry was a free safety and [[Punter (American football)|punter]] at [[Rutgers University]], intercepting a total of 9 passes over his three seasons, which he returned for 126 yards and two touchdowns. In 1979, he was named the team's MVP. In 1979 and 1980, Cherry earned [[Associated Press|AP]] All-East honors. In 1981, he was signed by the Kansas City Chiefs as a [[free agent]]  but was released in the final teams cuts. Cherry rejoined the club as a safety, and made his first career [[interception]] against division rivals the [[Oakland Raiders]].

Born in [[Riverside Township, New Jersey]], Cherry grew up in nearby [[Palmyra, New Jersey|Palmyra]], and played [[high school football]] at [[Palmyra High School (New Jersey)|Palmyra High School]].<ref>[https://www.njsportsheroes.com/deroncherryfb.html Deron Cherry], NJSports.com. Accessed April 9, 2024. "Deron Leigh Cherry was born September 12, 1959, in Riverside and grew up in Palmyra.... He attended Palmyra High School, excelling on the athletic field and in the classroom."</ref><ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20070930124949/http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=CHERRDER01 Deron Cherry]}}, Database Football. Accessed January 24, 2008.</ref> He was also on the high school basketball<ref>{{cite news|newspaper=[[Courier-Post]]|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/courier-post-deron-cherry-and-duane-cher/155067791/|title=Pals, Burl, Delran pull Freedom upsets|first=Ruth|last=Sadler|date=February 14, 1976|page=34}}</ref> and baseball teams alongside his brother Duane, with both Cherrys being selected for the local "All-Group 1" baseball team.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/courier-post/41609978/|newspaper=[[Courier-Post]]|title=Cherry Brothers, Mancini highlight All-Group 1 squad|date=June 10, 1976|page=61}}</ref>

Regarded as one of the best free safeties to have ever played the game, he was a six-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection from 1983 to 1988, [[Starting lineup|starting]] in five of them in his 11 years with the Chiefs. Few other Chiefs players have been selected to this number of Pro Bowls. He had six 100 [[Tackle (football move)|tackle]] seasons in his 11 years as a member of the Chiefs, with a career total of 927 tackles. He was a 5-time [[All-Pro]] in 1983, 1984, 1985, 1986, and 1988. He was also a five-time 1st team All-[[American Football Conference|AFC]] and two-time 2nd team All-AFC selection. Cherry's 15 career [[fumble]] recoveries place him in a three-way tie for the Chiefs record. He ranks third on the Chiefs list of most interceptions, and is only the 26th player in the history of the NFL to reach the 50 interception plateau. In 1987, he was selected to the Chiefs 25-year All-Time Team.

In 1987, he won the [[Byron "Whizzer" White NFL Man of the Year Award]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.football-almanac.com/awards/Byron_Whizzer_White_Award.shtml |title=Byron Whizzer White Award |access-date=2012-10-13 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120831153512/http://www.football-almanac.com/awards/Byron_Whizzer_White_Award.shtml |archive-date=2012-08-31 }}</ref> Prior to receiving this award, he was the Chiefs NFL Man of the Year selection in 1987. This is the most prestigious award given by the [[National Football League Players Association|NFL Players Association]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nfl.com/manoftheyear|title = NFL Man of the Year| website=[[NFL.com]] }}</ref>

He is actively involved in several civic organizations, including [[Special Olympics]], [[Muscular Dystrophy Association]], Project Warmth, Score 1 for Health, Camp Quality USA, and the [[United Negro College Fund]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2020}} For the past 25 years, Cherry has hosted his Celebrity Invitational.{{Citation needed|date=January 2020}} This tournament has raised over $3 million to support the children of the Kansas City area. Cherry is a frequent guest speaker at civic, charitable, and corporate events throughout the country.

In 1995, Cherry became a limited ownership partner in one of the NFL's then-new expansion teams, the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]]. This made him the first minority owner of an NFL franchise in the league's history.  Cherry is also a managing general partner with United Beverage, a local [[Anheuser-Busch]] distributor.

In 2019, the [[Professional Football Researchers Association]] named Cherry to the PFRA Hall of Very Good Class of 2019.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.profootballresearchers.org/hall-of-very-good-2019.html |title=PFRA Hall of Very Good Class of 2019 |access-date=September 14, 2019 |archive-date=January 23, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200123225213/http://www.profootballresearchers.org/hall-of-very-good-2019.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

He was selected by the Eagles in the third round of the [[2001 NFL draft]] where he spent four seasons before joining Oakland. During his four seasons with the Raiders, he twice received [[Pro Bowl]] honors and led the league in sacks in 2005. After one season with the [[New England Patriots]], Burgess rejoined the Eagles for his final season in 2010.

'''Derland Paul Moore''' (October 7, 1951 – September 24, 2020) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[nose tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[New Orleans Saints]] and the [[New York Jets]].  An [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]], he played [[college football]] for the [[Oklahoma Sooners football|Oklahoma Sooners]] and was selected in the second round of the [[1973 NFL draft]]. At the time he was drafted, Moore was the highest selected college [[walk-on (sports)|walk-on]] in the history of the NFL draft, a distinction overtaken by fellow Oklahoma Sooner [[Baker Mayfield]], the overall number one draft pick in 2018.  Moore went on to set a team record for service with 169 games played in 13 seasons with the New Orleans Saints, playing for five permanent head coaches and three interim coaches in that time.

He led the team in sacks in 1980, and was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] in 1983. Moore retired from the NFL in 1986 and was later inducted into the [[New Orleans Saints Hall of Fame]], the New Orleans Saints 40th and 50th Anniversary Team, the [[Missouri Sports Hall of Fame]], and was named as one of the Top 100 Sooners in Oklahoma University football history.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://newsok.com/centennial/topsooners|title=Top 100 Oklahoma Sooners|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071119131945/http://newsok.com/centennial/topsooners|archivedate=November 19, 2007}}</ref>

Moore died on September 24, 2020, age 68, from a lengthy illness.<ref>Sam Shannon, [https://www.neworleanssaints.com/news/new-orleans-saints-legend-derland-moore-dies-at-68 "New Orleans Saints legend Derland Moore dies at 68"], New Orleans Saints website, September 25, 2020</ref>

'''Derrick Shane Cullors''' (born December 26, 1972) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He was with the [[New England Patriots]] for four years, as a [[running back]] and [[kick returner]].

While only rushing for 149 yards in his entire career Cullors did play a significant role for the Patriots during the [[1997-98 NFL playoffs]]. With star running back [[Curtis Martin]] injured he helped lead the Patriots to victory over the [[Miami Dolphins]] during the Wildcard round. On a pivotal drive in the 3rd quarter, the first sustained scoring drive for either team, he contributed by carrying the ball 7 times for 42 yards, which ended in a field goal to give the Patriots a 17–0 lead. They would go on to win 17–3 as Cullors ended up being the game's leading rusher with 86 yards on 22 carries.

In 1998, he finished tied for third in the [[American Football Conference|AFC]], with 1085 yards on 45 returns.  Cullors scored his lone offensive NFL touchdown on a pass from [[Drew Bledsoe]] during a Week 13 victory over the [[Buffalo Bills]] in 1998. He also had an 86 yard kickoff return for touchdown against the Buffalo Bills in week 11 of the 1997 season.

'''Derrel Joe Luce''' (born September 29, 1952) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Baylor Bears football|Baylor Bears]], earning second-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors [[1974 College Football All-America Team|1974]]. He played six seasons in the NFL for the [[Baltimore Colts]], [[Minnesota Vikings]], and [[Detroit Lions]].

Luce got his NFL opportunity in [[1976 Baltimore Colts season|1976]] when starting linebacker [[Tom MacLeod]] was injured.<ref name=MG77>Wilt Browning (ed.), Baltimore Colts 1977 Media Guide. Baltimore, MD: Baltimore Colts Football Club, 1977, p. 31.</ref> Luce started all 14 games for the Colts during that season, registering 68 solo tackles and 4 assists, as well as the first two of his 3 career interceptions.<ref name=MG77 /> He also saw action on [[special teams]] on the punt coverage unit, recording three more tackles.<ref name=MG77 />

He was released by the Colts on August 22, 1979, immediately ahead of the [[1979 NFL season]], and was claimed off [[Waivers (NFL)|waivers]] two days later by the [[Minnesota Vikings]], for whom he saw action in all 16 games of the [[1979 Minnesota Vikings season|1979 season]].<ref name=TSNFR81>Howard M. Balzer (ed.), ''Football Register: 1981 Edition.'' St. Louis, MO: The Sporting News, 1981, p. 240.</ref> He made the Vikings roster again in [[1980 Minnesota Vikings season|1980]] but was released on October 1, after having appeared in four games.<ref name=TSNFR81 /> The [[Detroit Lions]] signed him two weeks later as a [[free agent]] and he appeared in the last 9 games of the season for the silver-and-blue.<ref name=TSNFR81 />

Luce received a [[Bachelor's degree|Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[Geology]] from Baylor in 1975 and subsequently enrolled in [[Baylor Law School]] towards the end of his NFL career.<ref name=TSNFR81 />
